name: Tretinoin microsphere (Retin-A Micro)

card.summary: A time-release tretinoin gel that delivers the retinoid more gently, used to clear acne and improve sun-damaged, uneven skin.
card.note: Prescription retinoid; can cause dryness and peeling and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

quick.overview:
Tretinoin microsphere gel (Retin-A Micro) is tretinoin encapsulated in tiny porous microspheres that release the drug gradually. It is used for acne and has been tested on photodamaged facial skin.

For appearance, the payoff is clearer pores, fewer breakouts and, in photoaging trials, improved skin texture and tone. The microsphere vehicle is designed to improve stability and tolerability compared with conventional tretinoin.
quick.how: Applied topically to the face as a gel, typically in the evening, as part of an acne or anti-aging routine, often with sunscreen by day and sometimes with other acne agents. Results build over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Redness, dryness, peeling and sun sensitivity are common. Tretinoin is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is a prescription product; irritation is the main tolerability concern.

lead: Tretinoin microsphere gel, sold as Retin-A Micro, is a formulation of tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid) in which the drug is held in microsponge particles. The design improves stability, since tretinoin degrades in light and with oxidisers, and was FDA-approved for acne in 1997.[1]

It helps looks by treating comedones and inflammatory acne and by reducing signs of photoaging. A placebo-controlled trial of the 0.1% gel in photodamaged facial skin enrolled 45 subjects over six months, followed by six months of open-label use.[2]
Comparative trials have tested it against adapalene gel for tolerability and efficacy in acne.[3][4]

chain: Normalised follicle turnover and less irritation
angle.text: The microsphere gel delivers tretinoin to treat acne and improve photodamaged skin with an eye to better tolerability.

paras: Acne is the approved use. Reviews describe topical retinoids as acting against comedones and microcomedones and having anti-inflammatory effects, and note that retinoids are often combined with antibacterials.[5][6] Photodamage has been studied in a placebo-controlled trial.[2]

In the photodamage trial, tretinoin microsphere gel 0.1% was compared with placebo for six months, with subjects then using the active gel in an open-label phase.[2] Two randomised trials compared it with adapalene gel 0.1% in acne, one a split-face tolerability and preference study.[3][4] A randomised study evaluated a 0.04% pump formulation in preadolescents with acne.[7] A trial in subjects of colour examined pigmentary changes when tretinoin microsphere was added to clindamycin-benzoyl peroxide therapy.[8] Reviews note it was compared with tazarotene and adapalene.[9]

Tretinoin breaks down with light and oxidisers; microsphere gel encapsulates it to improve stability.[1] Vehicle choice is considered important because the skin barrier may be impaired by acne and by treatments.[10]
Topical tretinoin can cause irritation, redness, peeling, dryness and sun sensitivity, and use during pregnancy is contraindicated because of birth-defect risk.[1]

timeline.event: FDA approves the microsphere gel for acne.[1]
